title: Standardizing Units and Formats
learning_outcomes: Explain standardizing units and formats and accurately refer to at least two syllabus subtopics.
Apply the main idea of standardizing units and formats to a small example, trace, calculation, or scenario.
Identify one important assumption or failure mode and describe how to check it.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study standardizing units and formats in the context of data cleaning and preprocessing. You will connect the PDF subtopics to a small example and practice describing what the evidence does—and does not—support.
content.why_it_matters: Standardizing Units and Formats matters because it affects how data is collected, represented, analyzed, interpreted, or used in a decision. Check the task and assumptions before choosing a method.

content_blocks.title: The central idea
content_blocks.text: Cleaning means making explicit, documented decisions about quality problems while preserving provenance and avoiding transformations that leak future information.

items.title: Measurement units
items.text: Define measurement units in relation to standardizing units and formats; identify the input, output, assumptions, and who uses the result.

items.title: Currency representations
items.text: Work through currency representations using a small, synthetic example before scaling up. State what the calculation or method returns and why that result is useful.

items.title: Number formats
items.text: Check the edge cases for number formats: missing values, unusual ranges, different groups, time boundaries, or a changed input can affect the conclusion.

items.title: Consistent categorical labels
items.text: Document the rule or choice for consistent categorical labels so another learner can reproduce the analysis and understand its limitations.

items.title: Unit-conversion validation
items.text: Define unit-conversion validation in relation to standardizing units and formats; identify the input, output, assumptions, and who uses the result.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: 1. Restate the question addressed by standardizing units and formats. 2. Identify the input data, intended output, and assumptions. 3. Predict what the small example should show before reading its output. 4. Change one input or assumption, compare the result, and document what remains uncertain.

content_blocks.code:
values = [10, None, 20]
observed = [v for v in values if v is not None]
print("missing:", values.count(None), "mean of observed:", sum(observed)/len(observed))

content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the provided synthetic input, rerun or retrace the example, and change one value at a time. Do not use personal records, credentials, or data you are not authorized to access.

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and fixes
content_blocks.text: Keep the question, data grain, units, and assumptions explicit. If a result differs, inspect the input and steps in order. Avoid turning an observed association into a causal claim, treating a sample as the population, or assuming a small demonstration guarantees production behavior. Dropping missing values changes the analyzed sample; document the choice.

content_blocks.title: Responsible interpretation
content_blocks.text: This example is a teaching aid. It is static in the CodeLeaf lesson and is not executed in the browser. It uses small synthetic values; validate any real workflow in a separate, appropriate local environment and protect sensitive data.

content_blocks.title: Recap and next step
content_blocks.text: Recap: Cleaning means making explicit, documented decisions about quality problems while preserving provenance and avoiding transformations that leak future information. hints: Write down the input, expected result, units, and assumptions first.
Change only one condition when testing a revised example.
Ask whether the data and method represent the real decision; do not infer causality or production readiness from a toy example.
